name: Apache Kafka
tagline: A replicated commit log that decouples producers from consumers, in order per partition.

howItWorks.title: KRaft brokers
howItWorks.body:
KRaft replaces ZooKeeper; controllers keep metadata in a Raft quorum.
A node runs as broker, controller, or both.
Each partition has one leader and follower replicas.
Producers and consumers talk to the partition leader.

howItWorks.title: Topics and partitions
howItWorks.body:
A topic is split into partitions, each an append-only log.
The record key hashes to a partition; same key, same order.
Partition count caps consumer parallelism in a group.
Partitions can be added later, never removed.

howItWorks.title: Consumer groups, offsets and lag
howItWorks.body:
Consumers in one group split the partitions between them.
Each group commits its own offset per partition.
Lag is log end offset minus committed offset.
Extra consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.

howItWorks.title: Latency tuning method
howItWorks.body:
Measure end-to-end latency and per-partition lag first.
Raise partitions, then consumers, until lag stops growing under load.
Re-test with the real key distribution; hot keys stay on one partition.
Stop when added partitions no longer cut latency.

howItWorks.title: Listeners and retention
howItWorks.body:
Clients connect to the bootstrap address, then to advertised listeners.
Listeners are plain TCP, so L4 balancers must not hide broker addresses.
Advertise a DNS name every client can resolve.
Retention deletes old segments by time or size, not by consumption.

howItWorks.title: What sits in front
howItWorks.body:
Platform services are producers: they send records to a topic through the bootstrap address.
Kafka Connect source connectors pull data from databases and files into topics.
One load balancer works for bootstrap only; every broker needs its own advertised address.
Users and the Edge stay outside; they reach Kafka only through application services.

howItWorks.title: What sits behind
howItWorks.body:
Consumers in groups read the log; sink connectors write topics into databases and object stores.
Behind the brokers sit local disks for log segments and the KRaft controller quorum.
On Kubernetes, the Strimzi operator runs brokers and exposes them by NodePort, LoadBalancer or Ingress.
JMX metrics go to Prometheus; authenticate with SASL or mTLS and restrict topics with ACLs.

howItWorks.title: Alternatives
howItWorks.body:
RabbitMQ: choose it for task queues, routing rules and per-message acknowledgement.
NATS: choose it for light, fast messaging with a small operational footprint.
Cloud queues (SQS, Pub/Sub, Kinesis): choose them when you want no brokers to run.
Redis Streams: choose it for small event flows when Redis is already deployed.

flow: The frontend serialises an event and picks a key.
The producer connects to the bootstrap address over TCP.
The broker returns metadata with advertised listeners.
The producer sends the batch to the partition leader.
The leader appends to the log and replicates to followers.
Backend consumers in one group fetch from their assigned partitions.
Each consumer commits its offset after processing.
Lag per partition shows whether consumers keep up.

deploy.summary: A single-node KRaft Kafka 3.7 broker in Docker on Linux with a DNS name and systemd.
prerequisites: Linux VM with Docker Engine 24+ and Compose v2
Static IP and a DNS record for the broker
Data disk with room for retention

steps.title: Prepare the host
steps.code:
sudo mkdir -p /opt/kafka && cd /opt/kafka
echo 'KAFKA_HOST=kafka.lab.internal' | sudo tee .env
echo '10.0.0.20 kafka.lab.internal' | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts   # or add an A record in DNS
sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/24 to any port 29092 proto tcp
steps.note: Placeholders: name, IP and subnet. Every client must resolve the name you advertise.

steps.title: Compose file
steps.code:
services:
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.7.0
    container_name: kafka
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "29092:29092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: INTERNAL://:9092,EXTERNAL://:29092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: INTERNAL://kafka:9092,EXTERNAL://${KAFKA_HOST:?set in .env}:29092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: INTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: INTERNAL
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
    volumes:
      - kafka-data:/var/lib/kafka/data
volumes:
  kafka-data: {}
steps.note: Save as compose.yaml. One node, replication factor 1, PLAINTEXT: lab only.

steps.title: Run under systemd
steps.code:
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/kafka.service >/dev/null <<'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=Kafka KRaft broker
Requires=docker.service
After=docker.service network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=yes
WorkingDirectory=/opt/kafka
ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker compose up -d
ExecStop=/usr/bin/docker compose down

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
UNIT
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now kafka.service
steps.note: The broker now starts at boot.

steps.title: Create a topic
steps.code:
docker exec -i kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create --topic orders.events \
  --partitions 6 --replication-factor 1 --config retention.ms=604800000

steps.title: Produce keyed events
steps.code:
printf 'o-1:created
o-2:created
o-1:paid
' | docker exec -i kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic orders.events \
  --property parse.key=true --property key.separator=:
steps.note: Events with key o-1 land in the same partition, in order.

steps.title: Consume in a group
steps.code:
docker exec -i kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
  --topic orders.events --group billing --from-beginning --max-messages 3 \
  --property print.key=true --property print.partition=true
steps.note: The group billing now owns committed offsets.

steps.title: Read offsets and lag
steps.note: Read CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG per partition.

steps.title: Match partitions to consumers
steps.code:
docker exec -i kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --alter \
  --topic orders.events --partitions 12
docker exec -i kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --topic orders.events
steps.note: Adding partitions changes key mapping for new records. Add consumers in the group until lag stops growing.

verify: Broker up: docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 | head -1
Group lag: docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group billing
pitfalls: A wrong advertised listener connects, then fails; clients follow the advertised host.
A plain L4 load balancer in front hides brokers; advertise each broker's own address.
More consumers than partitions leaves the extra consumers idle.
Partitions can grow but never shrink, and growth re-maps keys.
Retention deletes by time or size even if nobody consumed the data.
Replication factor 1 loses data when the broker disk fails.
Consumers that process slowly trigger rebalances; tune max.poll.interval.ms.
keyPoints: Topics split into partitions; order holds only within one partition.
Consumer groups share partitions; one partition feeds one consumer.
Offsets and lag show how far consumers trail the log.
Advertised listeners must resolve and route from every client.
quickDeploy: Run a KRaft broker with internal and external listeners
Create a topic with six partitions
Produce keyed events and consume them in a group
Read lag, then match partitions to consumers
osiNote: A binary protocol over TCP; clients reconnect to advertised hosts.
production: Run three KRaft nodes, replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2.
Size partitions for target throughput and consumer parallelism.
Set retention.ms and retention.bytes per topic; watch disk headroom.
Secure listeners with TLS and SASL; restrict with ACLs.
Alert on consumer lag, under-replicated partitions and offline partitions.
